summary:
Acre stands under Brazil's national framework, which applies in full in the state: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Justice Council resolution of 14 May 2013, joint adoption since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation.

Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018. There is no third-gender option on national identity documents, but civil registries have accepted "non-binary/unspecified" entries since 2020 and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. A trans visitor's documents and status are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity to be a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines; a Brazilian law firm's expatriate guide specifies terms of one to five years under ADO 26 and MI 4733. Acre carries protection at state level as well: a 2017 state anti-discrimination statute, with further state court rulings in 2025.

The statutory text does not describe what people meet. Brazil records one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, and the highest absolute number of killings of trans people globally, weighted away from the capitals. A legal assessment updated in April 2026 finds major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Brasília broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. That distinction applies within Acre, between Rio Branco and the state's interior.

Arrest carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires a judge to consult a person about their preferred placement, with male, female and LGBTI-specific units set out, and LGBTI status established by self-declaration at the custody hearing.
tangentialFactors:
OutRight International's country report, updated 12 March 2026, records that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, so the protective framework a visitor relies on is politically contested rather than settled.

Political visibility has risen alongside the risk. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections; in the same cycle close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle. Brazil's first transgender federal legislators were elected in 2022.

Targeted crime against LGBT people is documented in nightlife settings: a May 2024 investigation recorded drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo venues. General crime and city-safety conditions in Acre's towns are outside this record's scope.

Protection machinery has widened in the courts. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes. Commercial discrimination has also been litigated successfully: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman.
localsOnly:
Residents may register to vote under their lived name and identity even before identity documents are updated, and gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

Registry practice is wider than the document itself: civil-registry "non-binary/unspecified" entries have been possible since 2020, and the Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent, though no third-gender option exists on national documents.

Detention placement is governed by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021. LGBTI status is established by self-declaration before a judge, including at the custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted: the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a change of placement can be requested later, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the Rio de Janeiro state prison system, finding trans women housed in units operated as masculine, some in so-called neutral or security units, and describing placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 permitting people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

Case law from 2022 shows lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending Maria da Penha Law and Feminicide Law remedies to trans women.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Acre-specific figures on violence against trans or LGBT people, on hate-crime prosecutions, or on the treatment of LGBT detainees in the state's prisons appear in the available sources; the national violence data and the Rio de Janeiro prison census stand in as the closest evidence, and their transfer to Acre is an inference rather than a sourced finding.

The application of Acre's 2017 anti-discrimination statute in reported cases is not sourced. The state court rulings of 2025 are recorded in the national survey's state-by-state listing without the facts, parties or outcomes being described in the material available here.

Whether the National Council of Justice placement rules have been followed in Acre is unresolved on this record. The expatriate guide's assessment of social friction in smaller cities and rural areas is a general national observation and is not specific to Acre.

Entry and visa conditions for trans travellers, including recognition of foreign gender markers and any screening at airports in Acre, are not covered by the sources.
